questions.q: What is the main job of DNS?
options: Encrypting traffic between a browser and a server
Translating human-readable domain names into IP addresses
Assigning IP addresses to new devices on a network
Compressing web pages for faster delivery
questions.explain: DNS is a directory service: it maps names like northbridgeretail.com to the numeric IP addresses that routers actually use.

questions.q: In a DNS lookup, which server holds the real, official answer for a domain?
options: The root server
The recursive resolver
The authoritative name server
The stub resolver
questions.explain: The authoritative name server is the one that actually holds the domain's records and returns the real answer; everything before it is just routing the question there.

questions.q: Which DNS record type points one domain name at another domain name?
options: A
CNAME
MX
TXT
questions.explain: A CNAME record maps one name to another name, such as checkout.northbridgeretail.com pointing to northbridgeretail.com.

questions.q: What does a DNS record's TTL control?
options: How many devices can query that record at once
How long resolvers are allowed to cache the answer before re-checking
How many IP addresses a single record can hold
Whether the record uses IPv4 or IPv6
questions.explain: TTL, in seconds, tells caching resolvers how long they can keep using a stored answer before they need to ask again.

questions.q: Before migrating a service to a new server, why would a team lower that record's TTL in advance?
options: To make the record permanently uncacheable
To speed up how quickly the DNS change becomes visible everywhere once the cutover happens
To block the record from being looked up by outside resolvers
TTL has no effect on migrations
questions.explain: A shorter TTL set well ahead of a migration means cached answers expire quickly, so the real cutover propagates fast instead of trickling out over the old, longer TTL.
